name: Apophenia
statement: Apophenia is the tendency to find meaning and connection among unrelated things, a term Klaus Conrad coined for a stage in the onset of psychosis.
meaning: Conrad's term was clinical. In his 1958 stage model of beginning schizophrenia, apophany named the phase in which a patient's whole perceptual field fills with abnormal meaning. It arrives after a period of dread and before the sense that the world revolves around the self. Modern usage keeps the pattern-finding and drops the psychosis, treating apophenia as an ordinary trait on which people differ. The shift matters for the evidence, because the two versions are measured by different instruments: clinical interview on one side, false-alarm rates and questionnaire items on the other. Nothing links them except the name. Pareidolia, seeing faces in objects, is the visual special case and sits at entry 33. Judging streaks in random sequences is entry 60, the clustering illusion, and the stock-market experiment described below belongs to illusory correlation, entry 162.

origin.where: Die beginnende Schizophrenie: Versuch einer Gestaltanalyse des Wahns (Thieme Verlag, Stuttgart)
origin.note: Conrad's German Apophänie is rendered as 'apophany' by Aaron Mishara, whose 2010 account in Schizophrenia Bulletin is the source used here; the subtitle above is quoted by Hambrecht and Häfner. The book itself was not obtained. Archive.org holds no copy, Europe PMC holds none, and what Crossref holds under the title is two reviews of it published in 1960. Mishara describes a stage model built from a sample of 107 soldiers Conrad saw while directing a neurological military hospital, and gives the Greek derivation as apo, away from, plus phaenein, to show. The sentence defining apophany that everyone quotes is footnoted by Mishara to Conrad's 1959 article in Der Nervenarzt, not to the 1958 book.

evidence: Mishara describes apophany as the repetitive and monotonous experience of abnormal meaning across the entire surrounding field: being observed, spoken about, followed by strangers. Once it takes hold, he writes, no aspect of the field remains untouched. It sits between trema, Conrad's name for the stage fright of something important about to happen, and anastrophe, in which the patient becomes the passive middle point of a universe that revolves around him. Hambrecht and Häfner put the model to an empirical test on 267 first admissions in the ABC schizophrenia study. Trema was confirmed as the frequent first stage. The order Conrad proposed for the next two, apophany then apocalypse, was not, and they conclude that his model cannot completely be generalised. The laboratory literature is about individual differences instead. Brugger and Graves gave 40 students a task that induces superstitious responding, and those scoring high on magical ideation tested fewer hypotheses and ended up believing in more illusory contingencies. Fyfe and colleagues tested 63 healthy adults on three tasks. On the one that asked them to describe moving triangles, higher scorers on schizotypy and delusion-proneness spontaneously reported more associations in the random condition. The largest study is Blain and colleagues, who modelled apophenia as a disposition to false positives in 1,193 Human Connectome Project participants and 195 undergraduates. Latent psychoticism predicted the latent apophenia factor in both samples, the equivalent paths for false negatives did not, and neither conscientiousness nor neuroticism predicted it. The path from openness reached significance in the first sample only. Standardised coefficients running from the shared openness-psychoticism variance to apophenia were .61 to .75, while the correlations underneath them are small. Psychoticism items correlated with theory-of-mind false positives between .07 and .14 in the first sample, and positive schizotypy with semantic false positives at .20 in the second. Krummenacher and colleagues gave 200 mg of levodopa or placebo to 40 right-handed men, 20 reporting paranormal experiences and 20 sceptics, in a double-blind between-subjects design. Sceptics were less sensitive under levodopa than placebo, believers favoured false alarms over misses while sceptics showed the opposite preference, and levodopa lowered those decision preferences in both groups. Whitson and Galinsky ran six experiments on lacking control. Participants who lacked control reported 5.16 images that were not there against 3.47, a difference the paper itself calls marginal at t(34) = 1.76, p = .09. Their firmer results are elsewhere, at 2.92 against 0.92 images in a field of random dots, t(23) = 2.18, p = .04, and at an overestimate of bad news about the smaller company in a volatile market, 5.0 against 3.9, t(42) = 2.40, p = .02. The authors write that their studies did not involve large sample sizes. Van Prooijen and colleagues asked 264 American adults to judge patterns in random coin tosses. Pattern perception correlated with belief in existing conspiracy theories at r = .37, in fictitious ones at .44 and in supernatural claims at .38. The largest signal-detection test is Müller and Hartmann, who had 723 adults judge whether faces or houses were present in noise. One standard deviation more paranormal belief raised the chance of a false alarm by 9.43%, and went with lower sensitivity and a more liberal criterion. Conspiracy mentality and COVID-19 conspiracy belief moved false alarms only in the block where three trials in four carried a real signal.

replication.headline: The correlation between pattern-finding and psychosis-spectrum or conspiracy belief survives replication at about r = .16, while both causal accounts, control threat and dopamine, have failed in preregistered tests.
replication.detail: Van Elk and Lodder ran seven experiments on magical thinking, conspiracy belief, paranormal belief and agent detection, and found no effect of control threat on any of them. Twelve of their Bayesian tests gave positive evidence for the null and two gave weak evidence for it. One gave weak evidence for an effect running the wrong way. Control-threatened participants believed less in conspiracy theories, 4.9 against 5.3, t(231) = 2.62, p = .009, d = .34. Their sixth experiment put 36 people through the snowy pictures task under vignettes written to vary control, and found nothing, t(35) = .736, p = .47, d = .12. They also re-analysed the 55-study meta-analysis of compensatory control by Landau, Kay and Whitson. That paper's abstract gives r = .25, its results section and its table of moderators give .24, and its linear trim-and-fill estimate found no missing studies. Recomputing the standard errors produced a funnel plot with extreme asymmetry, Egger's test at Z = 5.397, p < .0001, and the standard error explained 64.8% of heterogeneity. The re-analysis itself gave r = .26, 95% CI [.22, .30], and trim and fill brought that down to r = .186, 95% CI [.133, .238]. The dopamine result has fared no better. Smith and colleagues gave 150 mg of L-DOPA with benserazide against placebo, within subjects and preregistered; 49 of the 76 people in the wider project sat the Snowy Pictures Task that Whitson and Galinsky used, and 48 were analysed. False alarms were 12.15% on placebo and 11.28% on L-DOPA, with a directional Bayes factor of 20.25 for the null, and Bayes factors of 14.48 for accuracy, 11.46 for d-prime and 6.37 for response bias. The correlational side holds up better. Sternisko, Delouvée and Van Bavel replicated Dieguez and colleagues' first study in the United States and Switzerland, recruiting 1,277 people and analysing 814 of them, 521 and 293. Their correlations ran between .03 and .15. Their meta-analysis of 55 effect sizes from 24 studies gave r = .16, 95% CI [.09, .22], with heterogeneity of I² = 87.12%. The estimate was .27 across 22 American effect sizes and .07 across 33 European ones, where the interval runs from -.00 to .14 and the authors call the result marginal. Knežević and colleagues report a robust positive relation between apophenia and psychoticism in three community samples, two Serbian at 127 and 256 and one German at 384, with openness either unrelated to apophenia or negatively related to it. Tagami and Imaizumi recruited 40 Japanese female undergraduates and analysed 35. Positive schizotypy predicted none of their measures across three experiments, with Bayes factors for the null above 4.03 in the first and above 3.55 in the third, and one inconclusive value of 2.54 for reaction time in the second. The nearest thing to a registered replication in this literature tests the theory rather than the perception: Hoogeveen and colleagues re-ran the control-threat effect on belief in a controlling God with 829 people in the Netherlands and the United States, and reported Bayes factors of 5.41 and 11.16 for the null.

study.cite: van Elk, M., & Lodder, P. (2018). Experimental Manipulations of Personal Control do Not Increase Illusory Pattern Perception. Collabra: Psychology, 4(1), 19.

limits: No effect sizes are printed in the structured fields, because the two sides measure different things. One is a Bayes factor for the absence of an experimental effect, the other a meta-analytic correlation across questionnaires, and pairing them would invent a comparison neither paper makes. Apophenia also has no single instrument. Snowy pictures, coin-toss judgements, semantic false positives and magical ideation scales all travel under the name, and a result on one carries no automatic weight for another. Sternisko and colleagues excluded Whitson and Galinsky from their meta-analysis on the ground that it does not measure randomness dismissal directly, which is a fair statement of how loosely the field is bounded. Three papers were read only as abstracts, and nothing beyond an abstract is taken from them here. Brugger and Graves and Fyfe and colleagues have no open copy listed by OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar or Unpaywall, and UCL Discovery, which holds a record for Fyfe, refused this machine. Krummenacher and colleagues is marked open at MIT Press and in the Zurich Open Repository, and on 17 August 2026 the first returned 403 and the second an anti-robot challenge. Knezevic and colleagues is still blocked at Hogrefe, and what this page uses is the abstract the publisher deposited at Crossref. Conrad's book was not obtained, so everything about him here rests on Mishara and on Hambrecht and Haefner. The searches were run on 17 August 2026 across Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed Central, OpenAlex, Unpaywall and archive.org. They turned up no multi-laboratory replication project and no registered replication report for any apophenia paradigm; the registered report they did turn up, Hoogeveen and colleagues, tests a different prediction of the same framework.
misreadings: The commonest error is to use apophenia and pareidolia as synonyms. Pareidolia is a false positive in face detection with a measurable latency; apophenia as now used is a disposition spanning perception and belief, and the evidence for one does not transfer. The second error runs in the other direction, treating Conrad as having described a universal human tendency. He described a stage in the onset of psychosis in soldiers, and the generalisation to healthy variation was made by later writers rather than by him. Even the clinical claim is narrower than it looks: the one empirical test of the stage model confirmed trema and could not confirm the order of the stages after it. Whitson and Galinsky's finding is still quoted as settled, usually as the claim that losing control makes people see patterns. Their own snowy pictures test came in at p = .09, seven experiments with Bayesian evidence for the null point the other way, the conspiracy result reversed, and the meta-analysis supporting the framework falls from .25 to .186 once publication bias is modelled. The dopamine story is told more loosely still, as though giving a sceptic L-DOPA turns him into a believer. Krummenacher reported that levodopa lowered sceptics' sensitivity and made both groups' decision preferences less extreme, and a preregistered test with a dose-controlled design found strong evidence for no effect on false alarms. Latent-variable models are also read as though they reported raw associations. Blain and colleagues put standardised coefficients of .61 to .75 between the shared openness-psychoticism factor and latent apophenia, and in the sample of 1,193 the manifest correlations between psychoticism items and false-positive rates run from .00 to .14, which is the size of the thing being modelled.

sources.text: Mishara, A. L. (2010). Klaus Conrad (1905-1961): Delusional Mood, Psychosis, and Beginning Schizophrenia. Schizophrenia Bulletin, 36(1), 9-13. The source for Conrad's 1958 stage model, the term Apophänie and the sample of 107 soldiers; read in full twice at PubMed Central. Conrad's own book was not read.

Hambrecht, M., & Häfner, H. (1993). 'Trema, Apophänie, Apokalypse' - Ist Conrads Phasenmodell empirisch begründbar? Fortschritte der Neurologie-Psychiatrie, 61(12), 418-423. The empirical test of Conrad's stage model on 267 first admissions in the ABC study; read as the abstract held by Europe PMC, the paper itself being in German and behind Thieme.

Brugger, P., & Graves, R. E. (1997). Testing vs. Believing Hypotheses: Magical Ideation in the Judgement of Contingencies. Cognitive Neuropsychiatry, 2(4), 251-272. Read as the abstract held by Europe PMC; no open copy is listed by OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar or Unpaywall.

Fyfe, S., Williams, C., Mason, O. J., & Pickup, G. J. (2008). Apophenia, theory of mind and schizotypy: Perceiving meaning and intentionality in randomness. Cortex, 44(10), 1316-1325. Read as the abstract held by Europe PMC; the UCL Discovery record for it is not open and the site refused this machine.

Blain, S. D., Longenecker, J. M., Grazioplene, R. G., Klimes-Dougan, B., & DeYoung, C. G. (2020). Apophenia as the disposition to false positives: A unifying framework for openness and psychoticism. Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 129(3), 279-292. The published article was read from the copy on the DeYoung lab's own publications page; correlations are from Tables 2 and 3 and the path range from the discussion.

Krummenacher, P., Mohr, C., Haker, H., & Brugger, P. (2010). Dopamine, Paranormal Belief, and the Detection of Meaningful Stimuli. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, 22(8), 1670-1681. Read as the abstract held by Europe PMC; the open copies at MIT Press and in the Zurich Open Repository would not serve this machine.

Whitson, J. A., & Galinsky, A. D. (2008). Lacking Control Increases Illusory Pattern Perception. Science, 322(5898), 115-117. Full text read from two independently hosted copies of the published PDF. The report prints degrees of freedom rather than group sizes; the supporting material online was not obtained.

Landau, M. J., Kay, A. C., & Whitson, J. A. (2015). Compensatory control and the appeal of a structured world. Psychological Bulletin, 141(3), 694-722. Meta-analysis of 55 studies, r = .25 in the abstract and .24 in the results and Table 4. Full text read from a scanned copy, so the figures quoted here are the ones that also appear in the abstract held by Europe PMC.

van Prooijen, J.-W., Douglas, K. M., & De Inocencio, C. (2018). Connecting the dots: Illusory pattern perception predicts belief in conspiracies and the supernatural. European Journal of Social Psychology, 48(3), 320-335. Study 1 figures read from the full text at PubMed Central.

Dieguez, S., Wagner-Egger, P., & Gauvrit, N. (2015). Nothing Happens by Accident, or Does It? A Low Prior for Randomness Does Not Explain Belief in Conspiracy Theories. Psychological Science, 26(11), 1762-1770. Read as the abstract held by Europe PMC; the study is described here through Sternisko and colleagues, who replicated its first study.
van Elk, M., & Lodder, P. (2018). Experimental Manipulations of Personal Control do Not Increase Illusory Pattern Perception. Collabra: Psychology, 4(1), 19. Full text read.

Smith, E., Michalski, S., Knauth, K., Tuzsus, D., Theis, H., van Eimeren, T., & Peters, J. (2024). Pharmacological Enhancement of Dopamine Neurotransmission Does Not Affect Illusory Pattern Perception. eNeuro, 11(7), ENEURO.0465-23.2024. Full text read; preregistered at osf.io/a4k9j.

Sternisko, A., Delouvée, S., & Van Bavel, J. J. (2022). Clarifying the relationship between randomness dismissal and conspiracist ideation: A preregistered replication and meta-analysis. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 102, 104357. Figures read from the authors' preprint at osf.io/3yfgz, which is the version Semantic Scholar lists as the open copy; the journal version at Elsevier refused this machine.

Tagami, U., & Imaizumi, S. (2020). No Correlation Between Perception of Meaning and Positive Schizotypy in a Female College Sample. Frontiers in Psychology, 11, 1323. Full text read at PubMed Central: 40 students recruited, 35 analysed across three experiments.

Knežević, G., Kušić, B., Lukic, P., Lazarević, L. B., & Keller, J. (2024). Can the "Shotgun Wedding" of Openness and Psychoticism Be Justified Based on Apophenia as the Disposition to Commit False-Positive Errors? Zeitschrift für Psychologie, 232(4), 255-268. The full text is blocked at the publisher; the sample sizes and findings used here are from the abstract the publisher deposited at Crossref.

Müller, P., & Hartmann, M. (2023). Linking paranormal and conspiracy beliefs to illusory pattern perception through signal detection theory. Scientific Reports, 13, 9739. Full text read at PubMed Central: 743 people completed the study and 723 were analysed.

Hoogeveen, S., Wagenmakers, E.-J., Kay, A. C., & van Elk, M. (2018). Compensatory control and religious beliefs: a registered replication report across two countries. Comprehensive Results in Social Psychology, 3(3), 240-265. The nearest registered replication of the compensatory control framework, on belief in a controlling God rather than on pattern perception; full text read.
